p: Yes.

Yes.

Good afternoon and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing on the Committee on Contracts with the Committee on Transportation Infrastructure joint with Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations. At this time, please silence all electronic devices, and no one may approach the dais at any time. Chair, we may begin.

[gavel] There we go. Good afternoon. We are finally beginning. Commissioner Ochoa has already made a joke that DDC isn't the only place that suffers from delays. The Council does too. We're happy to finally be beginning. My name is Lincoln Restler. I have the privilege of chairing the Contracts Committee. My good friend, Majority Leader Shaun Abreu, is our Co-chair as the Chair of Transportation Infrastructure. And my other good friend, Deputy Speaker Dr. Nantasha Williams, the Chair of Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations, is the third Co-chair of this hearing. Today's oversight hearing is on the delivery of capital projects in New York City. We're happy to be joined by DDC, DCLA,

DOT, MOCS, others. Unfortunately, the MTA isn't here today. They are the single worst agency at managing capital projects in New York State. They would have made you all look really good, but unfortunately they're not here to steal the show. Our 10-year Capital Plan totals over $170 billion and includes many thousands of planned capital projects. The city maintains 30,000 acres of parks, 1,600 schools, 55 cultural— 55 public buildings, hundreds of firehouses and police precincts, 6,300 miles of streets, 800 bridges and tunnels. Our Capital Plan funds affordable housing, cultural institutions, and so much more. Everything from planting a street tree to installing a new water main to building affordable housing is a capital project in New York City. We focus a lot on our city's expense budget and services, but our city's infrastructure and the capital projects needed to maintain and improve our public assets are essential to the operations of the city and the safety and well-being of all of us. A December report by the Comptroller's Office found that 80 percent of capital projects managed by the Department of Design and Construction were behind schedule by an average of 3.5 years. And capital

projects take on average 7.5 years. That's essentially the entire Mamdani administration, should he be reelected, to do a capital project. And New York City is paying more and more and more to build public infrastructure than any other city in the world. Over half the capital projects— over half the capital projects in New York City are over budget which costs $54 billion more than had been anticipated. It's shockingly hard to know exactly how far behind and how far over budget we actually are on our capital projects. The aforementioned comptroller's audit from the end of last year of DDC project management found that DDC does not track cost increases from project initiation to completion in its project management software. DDC also does not have a centralized place to find detailed budget data– to find detailed budget data maintained by individual project managers, which means there aren't effective mechanisms to mitigate delays and cost overruns as they emerge. As we are facing deficits on the expense side and potential cuts to our capital plan, it's critical that we identify all possible savings, including from excessive cost overruns of our capital projects. The city has limited tracking

of the state of repair of our infrastructure assets, resulting in insufficient capital planning and increasing costs as our schools and parks fall into a state of disrepair. Our libraries alone are facing $1 billion in repair needs, compounded by the fact that the average branch is over 60 years old. Today, we hope to gain a better understanding of what action is needed to limit delays and cost overruns. The prior administration's Capital Process Reform Task Force back in 2022 produced 39 recommendations, several of which remain outstanding. But it's not clear that the task force's work has led to any demonstrable improvement in capital project delivery. More recently, DDC agreed to a series of recommendations following Comptroller Lander's audit, and we look forward to updates on where those recommendations stand and how the new administration plans to improve our profoundly frustratingly— our profoundly frustrating and painstakingly slow capital project delivery system. Through procurement reform, expansion of design-build, and improved project management and planning, I am confident that we can complete projects on time and under budget. Before we begin, I do want to offer a very special welcome to

our new DDC Commissioner, Commissioner Ochoa. I've had the privilege of working closely with Commissioner Ochoa for many years, and he is a public servant of rare ability. I'm excited by the energy and creativity that you're going to be bringing to DDC. I'd also like to congratulate Commissioner Vij on your appointment. I have heard really terrific things about you from many mutual friends. Thank you also to representatives from MOCS and DOT for joining us today. I'd like to recognize the Contracts Committee staff for their hard work preparing for today's hearing: Senior Counsel Alex Paulenoff [sp?], our Legislative Counsel Jahari Frazier [sp?], Policy Analyst Alex Yablon [sp?], Financial Analyst Owen Kotowski [sp?], and my Chief of Staff, who is absolutely brilliant, Molly Haley [sp?]. With that, I'd like to turn it over to— do you want to go next? You want to go next? Sean? To Majority Leader Council Member Shaun Abreu for his opening remarks.

Thank you, Chair. Good afternoon and welcome to today's joint hearing of the New York City Council's Committees on Contracts, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations. I am

Council Member Shaun Abreu, Majority Leader and Chair of the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure. I would like to thank Chairs Restler and Williams and the staff of all three committees for their work in preparing for today's hearing. Today the committees will examine capital construction contracting and the persistent cost escalation and delays that affect the delivery of critical public infrastructure projects across New York City. We will also hear Intro 263 sponsored by Council Member Krishnan in relation to developing a strategic blueprint to reduce capital project durations by at least 25 percent, Intro 465, sponsored by Council Member Stevens, in relation to a study and report on the expansion of ferry service along the Harlem River, and Resolution 264, sponsored by Council Member Lee, calling on the state to grant permanent and expanded design-build authority to all New York City agencies. This oversight will focus specifically on why city capital projects often exceed their budgets and how existing procurement methods may be contributing to cost overruns. In addition, we will examine the time delays many projects experience. When these things happen, New

Yorkers ultimately pay the price through deferred infrastructure improvements, higher project costs, and longer waits for the facilities and services they depend on. This hearing will also come at an important moment. In 2019, New York State passed the Public Works Investment Act, PWIA, which authorized the Department of Design and Construction, DDC, and other capital agencies in New York City to use what is now known as traditional design-build-delivery on certain projects. In 2024, the PWIA was expanded to authorize DDC to use progressive design-build, which is a more streamlined method as opposed to traditional design-build on resiliency and infrastructure projects, and construction management-build, otherwise known as CM-build, on libraries and cultural institutions on city-owned land. And in addition, from 2022 through 2024, Mayor Adams' Capital Process Reform Taskforce issued 39 recommendations intended to modernize and improve the city's capital process. Today, we will assess how the city plans to continue to use these newer delivery tools and what progress has been made on implementing the reforms from the mayor's taskforce to improve capital construction going forward. DDC plays a

central role in this work as the city's primary capital construction manager, partnering with more than 20 agencies to deliver both public buildings and core infrastructure projects. At the same time, the Department of Transportation manages a vast portfolio of public assets, including thousands of miles of streets and sidewalks, hundreds of bridges and tunnels, traffic signals, signs, streetlights, and ferry facilities. When project delivery systems fail, the consequences impact nearly every part of our city. As we consider Intro 263 and Reso 264, we must look at how to shorten project timelines, but also at how to build a capital project— but also how to build a capital process that is more strategic and responsive to the city's infrastructure needs. I look forward to hearing from representatives of DDC, DOT, MOC, DCLA, industry stakeholders, and advocates about the causes of increasing capital construction costs, the status of current reforms, and the paths— the path forward for delivering projects more efficiently and effectively for New Yorkers. Before we begin, I'd like to thank my staff and the committee staff for their hard work in preparing for today's hearing. Jalissa Quigley [sp?], Theodore Miller, Sierra

Townsend [sp?], Kevin Kotowski [sp?], John Basile [sp?], Adrian DrePaul [sp?], and others. I would also like to thank Alex Paulenoff [sp?], Jahari Frazier [sp?], Alex Yablon [sp?], and Owen Kotowski from the Committee on Contracts, and Alejandro Carvajal [sp?], Regina Paul [sp?], and Carolina Gil [sp?] from the Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations. I will now pass it over to my co-chair, Deputy Speaker Dr. Natasha Williams.

Thank you so much, Majority Leader. It is a pleasure to chair the Committee on Cultural Affairs, Libraries, and International Relations, and I'd like to join my colleagues Chair Restler and Chair Abreu in welcoming everyone to this important oversight hearing. New York City's cultural institutions and libraries are the heartbeat of our city. Libraries, museums, theaters, galleries, art studios, and stages are the places where New Yorkers come to gather, learn, laugh, create, and build community and belong. The cultural sector is also a powerful economic engine that attracts millions of visitors to our city, employs more than 326,000 New Yorkers, and serves as a critical magnet for talent that employers in every

industry benefit from. Libraries, which are often called the most democratic spaces in our city, serve as a supportive and inviting environment that all New Yorkers benefit from, whether they are youngsters, teenagers, new parents, or older adults, and whether they are longtime New Yorkers or newly arrived migrants. Yet the process to build and maintain our critical libraries and cultural spaces is too often slow, opaque, cumbersome, and inequitable. Projects that should take months can take years. Projects that should take a year or two can last a decade. Projects that have secured funding can sit idle while they wind their way through a lengthy and uncoordinated approval process. Small organizations can be forced to front money that they don't have. Large organizations can be forced to carry interest costs on borrowed funds that divert resources away from their programming and hurt their credit. The result is a system that too often fails badly to serve the institutions that serve our city so well. We know that the process is broken, and now we must do what we can to fix it first. The capital construction process needs to be reformed. The city must bring clarity and accountability to a fragmented process by

publishing clear rules for how projects are assigned, align agency approval so they move in parallel instead of in drawn-out sequence, and expand the use of modern delivery methods like CM-build to shorten delivery timelines and lower costs. We must treat reimbursement and procurement delays as policy failures, and we must provide bridge financing, faster payments and deliveries, and significantly expanded upfront support. Second, the city must be transparent and accountable in how it plans and executes cultural and library capital projects. DCLA's cultural capital projects tracker, which has not been updated since 2021, must be updated in real time, and it must track every project from funding to scope to budget to timelines to, yes, even delays. Libraries and cultural institutions deserve to understand how capital projects around the city are proceeding, and the public deserves to know how its funds are being spent. Third, the city must be thoughtful and proactive in how it is deploying capital funds citywide. DCLA must establish and publish a rolling five-year capital plan that ensures that libraries and cultural institutions are being built, upgraded, and maintained in a way that is

efficient, equitable, geographically distributed, and responsive to the city's cultural needs. This is not just about construction or contracting or procurement. It is about equity, access, and the future for cultural life in New York. When a library renovation is delayed, a community loses access to a vital resource. When a cultural organization can't afford to navigate a Byzantine [sic] construction or procurement process, entire neighborhoods are left behind. We have the opportunity and the responsibility to build a capital system that works for everyone. The question is not whether we can reform it. The question is whether we will reform it. I would like to thank Priyanka [sp?], Shaquille [sp?], Alejandro [sp?], Regina [sp?], and Carolina for all their support in this hearing. I look forward to hearing the administration's testimony as well as testimony from our libraries and our cultural institutions as well as the public about these important issues. And with that, I will turn it back to Chair Restler.

Thank you so much, Deputy Speaker. A couple things. One, I would like to just acknowledge my many great colleagues who are

here with us today who have been here already: Council Member Phil Wong of Queens, Council Member Virginia Maloney of Manhattan, Council Member Jim Gennaro of Queens, Council Member Ina Vernikov of Brooklyn, Council Member Justin Sanchez of the Bronx, Council Member Gale Brewer of Manhattan, Council Member Selvena Brooks-Powers of Queens, Council Member Chi Osse of Brooklyn, Council Member Pierina Sanchez of the Bronx, Council Member Farah Louis of Brooklyn, Council Member Althea Stevens, Council Member Shahana Hanif of the Bronx— I'm sorry, Althea, I know, you know, Council Member Althea Stevens of the Bronx, Council Member Sandra Ung of Queens, Council Member Shahana Hanif of Brooklyn– if I missed you— if I missed anybody else, you have my apologies. I have to make a special request of administration officials to limit your testimony to five minutes each. So– and would Council Member Stevens like to speak on her bill for a moment? Okay, and then we'll go to testimony from the administration. Thank you very much. Council Member Stevens.

Good afternoon. I would like to first begin by thanking Chair Abreu, who pushed for this, and Restler and Deputy Speaker

Williams for convening this joint hearing today. I would like to take a moment to discuss Bill Intro 465. This bill pushes for a study and report on the expansion of ferry services along the Harlem River. In the West Bronx, where I represent, there are multiple neighborhoods that are considered transportation deserts. I believe those communities that lack transportation options are ideal places where a ferry stop could and should be located. In the past, New York City's Economic Development Corporation have expressed disinterest in expanding ferries across the Harlem River. Despite this, the West Bronx is still in need of alternative forms of transportation services. Congestion prices has exacerbated traffic in the Bronx, leading to an increase in vehicles and emissions in the area. Those unhealthy conditions are another factor underscoring the need for this study. We already know that when residents are provided reliable alternative forms of mass transportation, they will use it. As the city is working towards becoming greener, why wouldn't a proposal that would alternative [sic] these burdens be considered? It is important to highlight that there are parts of the city that have multiple ferry

stops. I won't say who. In wealthier districts, particularly in Brooklyn and Manhattan, even in the Bronx, the only two stops, Throggs Neck and Soundview, are likewise in areas with a higher medium area income and compared to the West Bronx. I would also like to note that ferry service along the Harlem River would be a great economic driver, as within the West Bronx lies Yankee Stadium, the Bronx Terminal, and a series of parks, making another path for the West Bronx to be a true connector to the city. Though we do not have a— though we do have a Metro-North stop, alternative forms of mass transportation is desperately needed. In closing, Intro 465 ensures community like the West Bronx is not left behind in the conversations of transportation equity and stability. A comprehensive study on the ferry expansion along the Harlem River Drive will provide data necessary to determine whether this investment can improve access, reduce congestion, and support economic growth in underserved communities. As New York City continues to prioritize climate goals and infrastructure improvement, we must also prioritize equity in how those resources are allocated. The West Bronx deserves meaningful consideration and

innovative solutions that connect residents to opportunities. I look forward to working with my colleagues and stakeholders to advance this conversation and bring greater transportation access to the communities that need it most. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Council Member Stevens, for that great effort. I once regrettably shared at an EDC oversight hearing how many ferry stops are in District 33, and she's never let me hear the end of it. So I applaud her efforts to expand more ferry service in the Bronx, where it's very much needed. With that, I will turn over to Committee Counsel to administer the oath of office.

We will now hear testimony from the administration. Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation. Panelists, please raise your right hand. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee— before these committees, excuse me, and to respond honestly to councilmember questions?
I do.
Alright, you may begin when ready.

Good afternoon, Chairs Abreu, Dr. Williams, Restler, members of the committee. I am Paul Ochoa, and I'm thrilled to be here today on day three of my new role as the Commissioner of the New York City Department of Design and Construction. I've had the pleasure of working with many of the members of this Council in my previous roles at DOT and City Hall, and I look forward to working together in this new capacity. I also want to thank Mayor Mamdani for entrusting me with this huge responsibility to deliver capital projects for the City. I am pleased to appear before you today to discuss the agency's ongoing efforts to reform the capital design and construction process. I am also joined by my colleagues at DDC, Jade Bailey, Acting Director of Alternative Delivery, Jeff Margolies, Associate Commissioner of Communications and Policy, as well as DCLA Commissioner Diya Vij, and representatives from DOT and the Mayor's Office of Contracting Services. The topics being discussed today are not just relevant, they are among my top priorities to tackle as new Commissioner. DDC began its current efforts to reform the capital delivery process back in 2018 under former Mayor Bill de

Blasio and then Commissioner Lorraine Grillo. In 2019, the agency published its initial strategic blueprint detailing roadblocks in the process and describing methods to resolve those issues. We have since published six updates to the blueprint, and in each one, we describe progress made, hurdles that remained, and how we can continue to collaborate with our partners. While we still have a long way to go, we have made great strides since 2018, including on-time delivery of the Bushwick Health Center for DOHMH, transforming Del Valle Square in the Bronx, completing Blue Belt— Blue Belts in Staten Island to manage stormwater, opening the amazing downtown Far Rockaway Library, and welcoming prospective pet owners to the Manhattan Pet Adoption Center. Now let me turn your attention to Intro 263 by Councilmember Krishnan. The bill requires DDC to produce a plan to reduce average project durations by at least 25 percent, including by standardizing processes and working towards better private utility coordination. As I mentioned before, faster delivery timelines are not— are one of our most important priorities. And Mayor Mamdani and Deputy Mayor Kerson have made it clear they share this goal. I would like to work with

the Council to come up with an ambitious plan to do just this. There are, however, a few items I would like to discuss about how the bill is written. For example, I would like to agree on what a good baseline should be for the wide variety of projects DDC manages. A one-size-fits-all approach would be an oversimplification of DDC's portfolio. I'm glad Intro 263 also calls out the need for better coordination with utilities, which I agree can be improved to avoid delays. One program that enhances this effort is joint bidding, which is governed by state law and allows the city to include private utility interference work in the same contract as the city's sewer, water main, and street upgrades. The program brings the private utilities to the table during the design phase of a capital project, encouraging collaboration and pre-engineering to help identify their underground lines so we can avoid delays when we opened up streets. The current joint bidding law expires at the end of this year, and we would appreciate the Council's support as we seek a long-term extension for this critical measure. There is another factor I'd like to bring up, and I did this quite often at DOT, which are the often

necessary scope changes. Capital projects shape our streets, improve our sewers, and create long-lasting community epicenters in libraries and rec centers. It is normal for agencies to want to add scope to projects since they only get one bite at the apple. I do not consider the consequences of these decisions cost overruns or delays in the traditional sense. We do also recognize that internal challenges at DDC remain, and we were always looking to learn from experience, all while tackling the ever-growing portfolio to deliver results for New Yorkers. This, of course, includes providing additional trainings for staff, regular updates to design specifications and contracts, new project risk management, management initiatives, and of course industry engagement. There is always more work to be done. I'd like to take a second to talk about alternative delivery. In DDC's past blueprints, we have always had a combination of suggested reforms to the current system and larger outside-the-box thinking ideas. One of the most important– one of those efforts is alternative delivery projects, which is the use of different contracting models outside of the state-mandated lowest-bidder system. Getting

permission in Albany to use these alternative delivery methods has been a game changer, and we appreciate the Council's support in giving us all the tools available to deliver faster. I am pleased to report that we have reached a tremendous milestone in our design-build portfolio. Just earlier this year, we opened the Shirley Chisholm Rec Center in East Flatbush. It was completed in just under three years, which is about half the time needed for a similar public buildings project using design bid build. The $141 million project was on time and also on budget. It is a stunning example of what we can collectively achieve for our city. We expect all five of our original design-build projects to be completed by the end of 2026, including the Brownsville Multi-Service Center, the Greenhouse and Community Center in Marlboro Houses in Brooklyn, and the Mary Daily [sic] Dalton Rec Center in Staten Island. I will just borrow two minutes from DCLA. Testimony is very short. We are rolling out the first Construction Manager Build, CM-Build, project, another alternative delivery method. We were also clear— we were clear to use CM-Build by the state in 2024 for library and cultural projects. CM-Build allows us to bring in a

construction manager to work with the designer, allowing for earlier collaboration to assess existing building conditions and construct availability and one entity to oversee all trades during construction. We feel this is a good portfolio for CM-Build because the libraries and buildings that house cultural groups tend to be older and require extensive renovations, which CM-Build is suited for. CM-Build was essential during the pandemic and the migrant crisis when we used it to build vaccination centers, COVID Centers of Excellence, and shelters in record times. We currently have one project that will be awarded shortly at 70 Mulberry Street with another six additional projects in various stages of scoping and procurement. Capital process reform, as was mentioned– under the last administration, City Hall created a process to look at reforms and recommendations for capital delivery. It included members of the Comptroller's Office, industry partners, agencies, and contractors. As Executive Deputy Commissioner at DOT, I was their lead on the capital reform task force. The final report and recommendations are worth reading, and many have already been implemented by us and our sister

agencies. Some of our biggest successes include expanded work allowance,— skip the definition— advanced capital planning, and a lot of legislative successes in Albany. Again, we look forward to continuous dialogue on how to best improve other capital delivery process. And thank you again for this opportunity to testify, and I welcome any questions you may have. And thank you, Commissioner, for let me borrowing some of your time.

Thank you, Commissioner Ochoa. Oh, and may— just before you begin, Commissioner, I'd like to thank Council Member Shekar Krishnan of Queens, Council Member Crystal Hudson of Brooklyn, and Council Member Chris Marte on Zoom for joining us. Thank you.

Good afternoon, Deputy Speaker Dr. Williams, Chair Abreu, and Chair Restler, and members of the committees. I'm Diya Vij, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs. Later I'll be joined by DCLA's Assistant Commissioner of Capital, Andrew Burmeister. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. Over the past month, my first as Commissioner, I've learned an incredible amount about the complex

process of cultural capital construction. I also come to this position as a cultural worker who experienced firsthand being part of a team that opened a major museum capital expansion project managed by DDC. Through ongoing discussions with cultural organizations, the expert team at DCLA, and the Deputy Speaker, it's been made clear that while the city's capital investments in cultural organizations are essential to keeping our sector thriving, there are definite challenges in this process that we are committed to addressing. Both Commissioner Ochoa and I recently began our positions under the mandate from Mayor Mamdani to address the affordability crisis and ultimately to make government work better for New Yorkers. No other city in America invests in its cultural infrastructure at this scale. In New York City, over the last 25 years, more than 500 cultural capital projects valued at $2.5 billion have been completed. These projects, large and small, have changed the face of our city and have brought high-quality cultural infrastructure within reach for millions of New Yorkers. Some recent examples drive home the magnitude of their impact on our city: the new home of the Studio Museum in Harlem, which opened

last fall; the renovated Delacorte Theater in Central Park; the renovated Hunterfly Road Houses at Weeksville Heritage Center in Brooklyn; a new welcome center at Greenwood Cemetery in Brooklyn; the renovation of the Poppenhusen Institute in Queens, the renovation of the Bronx River Art Center, improvements across the Snug Harbor campus on Staten Island, and a major renovation at Pioneer Works in Brooklyn. And these are just a few marquee examples. Through the city's support for capital equipment projects, there are theaters with new lighting, gardens with new vehicles, concert halls with new pianos, and so much more across the city. It's worth noting the ways that DCLA's capital program is unique and distinct from other city agencies. We are not creating our own assets. Cultural capital projects are assets for nonprofit organizations with their own boards, their own facilities plans, and a widely diverse set of needs. The projects we support are incredibly unique from one another. Cultural facilities require very specialized systems for very specific users. They are also often located in older buildings, which can pose a wide range of challenges for major capital upgrades. We can work with DDC to

plan and strategize for contingencies, but in the end, we can only learn what lies behind a century-old wall when it's knocked down. We're proud that a majority of our capital projects are infrastructure-related, upgrading HVACs and fire systems, replacing roofs or boilers, and so on. These mission-critical projects are rarely funded privately. DCLA has– also has a unique role in the capital process. We are funder, and we act like an owner's rep for our cultural organizations. Each year, we solicit requests from eligible groups, listen to the needs of the sector, talk with our partners in the Council and Borough President's offices, and determine where to invest these public dollars. From there, DCLA acts as a liaison between the cultural organization and the managing agency, most often our partners at DDC, and attends all construction and design meetings. We are an advocate and a thought partner for cultural organizations from the beginning to the end of the process. As the funding agency, we work closely with the managing agency as they determine the project budgets and timelines. DDC's front-end planning process is rigorous. It helps to determine much of the contours

of a project. But again, especially in older buildings, there are always unknowns you can't account for. I want to highlight several ways we've been working to improve capital delivery timelines for our constituents. Equipment times: through a batch procurement approach and other improvements, we've been able to reduce the time from allocation to an organization receiving equipment by six months in recent years. Exploring new approaches: we've recently started working with HPD to create cultural spaces as part of larger affordable housing developments. For projects like Indie Space in Chelsea and Belongo Afro-Latin Jazz Alliance in East Harlem, this will mean that they're able to move into fully built facilities a year faster than if these assets were created as a separate project. Capital feasibility planning: This new DCLA program works with smaller and mid-sized institutions before they embark on major capital projects. Helping to ensure what— that when they do start a project, they're ready to hit the ground running. I also want to echo Commissioner Ochoa's excitement for the major reforms being pushed by DDC, including CM-Build, which we expect will provide major benefits to cultural

organizations. We're grateful to our partners in state government for making this step possible and look forward to working with them on ways we can build on these reforms to reach even more organizations. It is also worth noting that our capital projects are still subject to the many realities we're facing today. Rising costs, tariffs, and foreign conflicts can all impact a project that's dependent on fuel, shipping, and materials from around the globe. IT equipment, for example, has gotten more difficult and costlier to procure as the competition for chips increases worldwide demand. Still, there's nothing better than cutting the ribbon on a new cultural asset that will welcome New Yorkers for generations to come. We're grateful to our partners at DDC for their work to bring these projects online and their continued partnership on out-of-the-box thinking on ways we can improve the process for everyone. Thank you again for the opportunity to testify today. I'm happy to answer any questions.

Thank you both for your testimony, even if those borrowed minutes kind of disappeared, I guess, somewhere between the

trade-off. I'll first turn it over to Chair Williams for her questions.

Thank you, Chair. The first question I have is on the capital construction process and— or first set of questions. So can you map out the process for cultural capital projects managed by DDC from initial proposal to closeout and payment? What are some of the common sticking points that add time to the process, and are there any meaningful process differences when it comes to library capital projects?

Thank you, Chair. I'm happy to take it from DDC front and then if DCLA has anything to offer, please jump in. So the way it works, and this is the way we take in any capital project for any sponsor agency, we receive what is called the capital initiation package, which essentially includes the scope, the requirements, the expectations of the projects from the sponsor agency. DDC then takes it into a front-end planning team which does rigorous review of the capital project initiation package, and we look at cost, estimated cost, estimated timelines, scope, feasibility. And this is really the back and forth that the

Commissioner Vij was mentioning, where we hammer out the details so that once we put it out for a bid for, for design or preliminary design depending on the delivery project, we are well ahead of time in terms of planning. And so once we get the CPI, we put it out to the market, we determine the type of delivery that we use. We always look at using alternative delivery methods for these types of projects. And then from there, we go through the entire design process, construction process, and finally closeout.
And the other question is, like, are there any common sticking points, and is the process different for libraries?

Yeah. So, this is— we mentioned— we both mentioned CM-Build. It is a new alternative delivery method. It works really, really well for renovations. We are very excited to implement it in a lot of the library projects. The new– whenever we are building a new library, for example, we tip— Far Rockaway is a great example. The challenges are a little different. A brand new building, we know sort of what is there, what is not there. And so we haven't run into huge issues whenever there's new buildings. But for renovations,

it can be complicated. I would also mention a lot of these spaces require at least some portion of the cultural institution to remain open during renovations, which just makes the actual work being done a bit more complicated.

Thank you. For DCLA, can you give the committee a feel for the volume of capital requests that come to DCLA each year? For example, how many requests are for state of good repair, energy upgrades, modernization, or expansion? And how does the dollar amount of requests compare to the dollar amount of projects funded?

Yeah, yeah, happy to share. So we just received all capital requests for FY27, and there are approximately 139 projects from 112 organizations totaling just over $683 million. Within that, there are 71 requests for construction, 21 related to good repair, 12 for energy projects, 38 for expansion projects. In FY26, just to give you a sense of what's funded, we received requests for 123 projects from 108 orgs, just over $671 million, and the city funded $282 million. In FY25, the request totaled $213.8 million. Oh, sorry, the request totaled $585 million, and the city funded $213.8

million. So it ranges between, like, 35 to 40 percent of projects funded.

Yeah, we noticed that, like, while there are many projects being funded, the dollar amount was low compared to, like, the total cost of what was requested. Okay, thank you. So how does DDC coordinate with DCLA and provide timeline updates to the agency? How does DDC account for the unique challenges that cultural organizations present, such as limited ability to close, the need to plan around performance seasons, or the need to make improvements to stay modern and viable? A lot to echo there. So, listen, both of the teams are in constant coordination, and that includes both DCLA staff, as the Commissioner mentioned, but also the, the individual cultural institutions who are the sp— also the sponsors of this project. A lot of this coordination happens through the front-end planning process. But also, listen, we are not a black box. DDC throughout the design, either preliminary design, final design, and up to construction, we are talking constantly to sponsor agencies, especially if we're seeing anything that wasn't expected in the project. We do run into unfilled field conditions. As the

Commissioner mentioned, it is much easier to know what the wall will have if it's a brand new building, but these old buildings have the same issue as a lot of our street reconstruction projects, which, you know, New York City is a very old city. We don't always know what is underground until we dig it up. And those are the types of conversations we have with our sponsor agencies, whether it's DCLA or another sponsor agency.

Can I just add also that, DCLA, our specific role in these conversations is as advocate of cultural organizations, and we're acutely aware of how they do business and the need for them to stay open as long as possible without jeopardizing their future programming. So our role in these meetings is really to understand the nuances of how cultural organizations do business and make sure that the process aligns.
Thank you. What are the most common coordination failures you see between agencies, contractors, or scopes, and how does this impact timelines?

You know, my answer would have been very different a week ago when I was

at DOT, than it is at DDC. No, listen, I think having very clear scopes and requirements is very, very important, and we— having that up front is critical. I also acknowledge that we can improve communication between DDC and our sponsor agencies to make sure that if we run into issues, we get prompt answers. I think that the thing that frustrates, you know, sister agencies or sponsor agencies is not hearing back if there is an issue. And so you have my commitment, and our sister agencies have our commitment that we're going to be very upfront about what is missing, if anything's missing, to make sure that we move projects along. I think the goal is for front-end planning to move those projects out for, for bidding and that's my commitment. And so if there's anything on the back end that I will do, that I can do, and the DDC can do, we will do it that.

Yeah, I'm also very interested in how DCLA determines the priority of projects. So if you can share that, and then in turn, like, DDC also has a long laundry list of various projects across many agencies. So how do you all also, like, determine priority of projects?

We evaluate projects based on how ready they are. If they're fully funded, we can move them to DDC. If the scope is clear, we can move them to DDC. And we are— sometimes that takes years to fund a project, but we're really looking at what— when the– we're working very closely with organizations as they go through that process to define scope and understand what it looks like to enter these processes. So priority for us is really the organization. Do they have the capacity? Are they ready to hit go on this project? And how then will they best manage it moving forward?

Yeah, and for DDC this prioritization is important. However, we have dozens of very, very experienced engineers and project managers. Anytime we receive a CPI, which is the capital initiation package, again, it goes to the front-end planning and it gets assigned to a project manager. We have— we can— we take on multiple projects at a time. From multiple sponsor agencies. And so, I'm not aware of any queue issues or having to prioritize based on staffing challenges. We take multiple projects at any given time from multiple sponsor agencies. What causes a cultural or library

project to require design? For example, a new boiler? Why would that need a full design and architectural renderings?

You know, the– it is hard to know, um, and especially in old buildings, exactly where the conduit's going to be, where the cabling is going to be. And so all these projects, even if they seem minor, do require some form of design. We mentioned CM-Build. I think that will make a lot of the delivery much faster because you have a construction manager up front who knows how to carry on these types of tasks, especially for renovation. So, I'm happy to report back as soon as we deliver our first CM-Build project, but that's exactly what it's meant. So we have a construction manager up front in the building working with the trades so that we can speed up the process.

Yeah, and I agree with you. You said some design is needed, but currently they have to do like full designs with architects. And so, like, yeah, like, maybe there needs to be some planning, but like a full design and architect for a boiler—

[interposing] Yeah, this is why the alternative delivery method is so important. If it wasn't for the alternative delivery authorization that we got in Albany, we would have to— we are required by the charter to have full designs for any capital project. I would also say as part of the CP process, which is the certificate to proceed process approvals, you do need a good sense of what the project will be. And so I agree with you, council member, and listen, we'd be happy to walk you through CM-Build. We have one project underway, but I think it's a really important conversation. So not just for you as a council member, but also for the cultural institutions to know what is required of them so that we can move projects faster.

What are the guidelines for self-management versus going through a capital agency for cultural projects? What rubric does DCLA use to decide, and how is it decided whether DDC or EDC will manage the process?
Thank you for that question. I'm gonna— I'm joined now by Assistant Commissioner of Capital Andrew Burmeister.

Hi. Self-management is a process we take pretty seriously. It's, I think, one of the highlights in our capital program. However, managing a project— for an organization to manage a project individually, that organization remains responsible for compliance with all of the laws and policies that a DDC-managed project would have to comply with, including prevailing wage, vendor integrity, payroll reporting, various local laws, things like that. So it's a tremendous burden to put on an organization. We do evaluate organizations when we decide whether they'd be appropriate for self-management. We look at whether they execute– have a successful execution of their mission. We look at the engagement of their boards. We look at the effective leadership and like, low turnover of administration and staff. Self-managed projects require a significant private top contribution, typically 50 percent. So we look for organizations that are able to privately fundraise. We look for organizations that have the capacity to fully finance the project, cover cost overruns, lay out funds in advance, and await

reimbursement. And we look for organizations that have a capital campaign plan with realistic goals.
And the DDC versus EDC, how do you all determine which projects go to which?
We actually don't make that determination. Our default is our partner at the Department of Design and Construction. Occasionally we partner with EDC. That is at their discretion.
So when do you decide to partner with EDC versus DDC? Is it DDC that's sending a project?
We will propose projects to EDC, and if they choose to take them on, they will take them on.
Okay. Is it possible to create guidelines for a cultural project to be self-managed?

Absolutely. We're always available. When we talk to organizations about self-management, we talk to them about what those responsibilities are, and we're

always available to help them get past that threshold of capacity in order to self-manage projects.
But can you, like, create, like, a document like a— how you just went through, like, the rubric, like, can you create a document like that for cultural institutions to have?
We'll certainly look into that. I think what we find is that the biggest obstacle is the private fundraising.
Okay. The front-end planning process doesn't seem to be working. Has the city considered any new approaches to avoid delays in cost escalation?

Let me defend front-end planning. I actually really, really like it. I know it can be frustrating from a sponsor agency perspective, from our cultural institution, but the more planning we do up front, the faster it is throughout– for us to put it out for a design, preliminary design, final design, and eventual construction, depending on the type of delivery. So it's really, really important. This is the– this is the process in which we answer a lot of questions. We also question a lot of the assumptions that the

sponsor agencies are making. Sometimes we get, you know, package– capital initiation packages that we think maybe are undershooting some of the costs or undershooting some of the requirements, or they miss something that could be added. The whole reason why DDC was created— and I know we're talking about cultural, but let me move to— move on to the streets for a second. The whole reason why DDC was created was to combine scopes. And so it is a really, really important process. I hear some of the frustrations, but in my mind, the, the more work we do on the front end, or the more planning work we do on the front end, the easier the project will be once we put it out for design and construction.

Yeah, off script a bit, not in my prepared questions, which this is like my constant question to many agencies. I think from a government perspective, like, things seem good, but like, no one actually asks the people who are like engaging with government that way. So, I'm just wondering, do you do like, focus groups or something to actually get feedback–
[interposing] Yeah.
outside of, like, getting regular feedback when you're dealing with a particular entity because like you say it's going fine, but other people say different. And so I'm just wondering–
[interposing] Sure.
like, do you create space for people to actually, like, co-create and like think of solutions that maybe you don't see on the agency side?

I think that's a very fair point. Listen, and I joked about having a different answer just last week, but as I'll put my former DOT hat on, whenever we had challenges or proposals, we brought them up to DDC. I think also Deputy Mayor Kerson is holding roundtables with all Commissioners, and she's very focused on project delivery. And I welcome feedback from our sponsor agencies on things how we can improve. I'm not saying it is a perfect process. I am saying it works, and it is important for us to do that. But I take your point well, and I'm happy to hear feedback of any potential improvements.

Yeah, like, even, like, in my case, like, the cultural institutions and the libraries themselves, so not just, like, with your sister agencies, but also the entities that have to manage these projects. Like the Commissioner said, it's a little different for cultural institutions. It's not another city agency that's co-managing the project.
Yep.

These are, like, essentially, you know, public-private partnerships and it's like a huge— the private is a huge component of the public and it doesn't seem like the public thinks of it that way in terms of like engaging and thinking through ways to solve problems. And maybe you are, but that's just my question. Like, are you doing that? Are you actually, like, receiving feedback in a tangible way to inform your practices?

Yeah, that's fair. What I will commit to you– it is day 3, but I'll commit to you, what I mentioned about the sister agencies, I– you're right, I was talking about other government entities. I will create space for us to hear from the cultural institution as well. I think

it's important and they are part– key partners. And so, you know, we already have a process for departments and other agencies. I will create a process if one doesn't exist. So for folks at DDC, if we already have one, I will be attending those meetings to hear directly from cultural institutions. So that includes the libraries, which are key partners as well.

Thank you. It can take several years to secure funding needed for critical capital improvements. Once an organization gets into scope development and contract, especially for projects that require multiple years of fundraising, the budget often does not keep up with the inflation costs, causing further delays, scope reduction, or additional rounds of fundraising, thus creating a never-ending cycle of requesting and falling short. How can DCLA and DDC work together to solve this issue?

You want me to take it? I can start it, and then, Commissioner, can add anything else? Listen, when I mentioned about doing more work up front, a lot of these CPIs, or Capital Initiation Packages, come with an estimate of what

the project will be, and we also at DDC come up with an estimate. Sometimes there's a discrepancy between what we think it'll cost and what the sponsor agency will cost, but then the ultimate decider is what the market decides. And so once we put it out for bid, that is the ultimate price. We are– you know, we can try our best to estimate based on past projects, but at the end of the day, we are sort of beholden to what the market puts out. There are escalators in every contract for things like tariffs and cost increases, but the things that are not– you know, the things that do happen are scope changes, as you mentioned, which do come with cost. I mentioned in my testimony, I don't consider those your typical cost overruns that people are sort of frustrated with. Those are just changes that the sponsor agency is requesting. And I think it's important for us to provide space for that. Would it be better if we limited them or have them upfront? Yes, but it does happen. And I'm not going to fault the sister agency for wanting to add something else.

Yeah, I think specifically for the cultural institutions, it's very frustrating because the whole purpose of, like,

leveraging some of these DCLA capital dollars is to use it almost as, like, a fundraising tool to get money from the private sector. And so I was hoping that you would say that you would continue to work to expedite the process, because a part of the problem is, is that when these institutions go to request money, and/or they start the process, because of the many delays that are well documented that is what creates sort of a compiling issue around funding. So, I mean, I thought you would—
[interposing] I see–

And to me, like, even thinking of, like, you all mentioning your testimony, this idea of affordability, well, like, when government is slow and archaic and bureaucratic, it actually makes these projects less and less affordable because the costs are so high. So, which to me goes back to self-management. Most of the institutions, if they can manage their own projects, they do it faster and cheaper. I don't understand why, like– I mean, I do understand it's laws, etc., you explained it, but I'm hoping that we can continue to, like, do our best to expedite projects so they do not–
[interposing] Sure.
rise in cost.

Listen, I would welcome, and if you want to host a roundtable, I'm happy to join. I think what I was talking about, the cost, and maybe it's a different way of looking at cost, is the expectation from a cultural institution that an upgrade will cost X. Once we get it at DDC, we think it will cost X times, you know, 1.3 and that could be considered— I think if I were a cultural institution, I would see that as a cost overrun or as higher than anticipated, but that is just based on our experience, and we are very experienced at delivering projects, and we're very attuned with what the market rates are. That is the cost. And so, I think that that's the distinction I was trying to make, but I think you're right. I think more communication is important, and if you want to host a roundtable, I'm happy to attend and bring in some of our folks from both the front-end planning and project managers to share best practices of what we've seen works, what doesn't. I would also echo some of our folks from DCLA mentioned, it is a lot of work to self-manage. And I want to make sure that

that is the point is made across. There's a lot of requirements, there's a lot of environmental work, DOB approvals, other agency approvals, sometimes DC, sometimes LPC, and so it's something that we are good at, it's something— this is why we are the project delivery agency, but I think, you know, we're happy to have those conversations, but we would just want to make sure that if cultural institutions are undertaking that, they know well and upfront what they're getting into.
Yeah, I'm happy that you also mentioned LPC because many cultural institutions are landmarks–
[interposing] Yeah.

which present other challenges and complexities. Okay, I'm gonna ask one more question for now, because there's so many people I'm sure that have a ton of questions for you. For the 39 cultural institutions that are CIGs and other arts organizations housed in city-owned property, how does DCLA or the city in general assess the condition of the buildings, systems, and capital equipment?

Yes. We have annual AIMS reporting, and every three years there are full

inspections of the facilities, and that is delivered to the institutions. I think that can be used— it's not currently, but it can be used as a planning document. And there are many opportunities for us to come together with leadership of SIGs to sit down and go through those and figure out what capital planning might look like for them together.
Thank you, and I will definitely be taking you up on your offer to host a roundtable.
Thank you so much, Chair Williams. We'll pass it to Chair Abreu, followed by Council Member Sanchez.

Thank you, Chair Restler. Commissioner Ochoa, congratulations on being appointed as Commissioner of DDC. Really exciting. I know you have just started, so I appreciate you joining us today and look forward to working with you to ensure that DDC builds better, faster, and cheaper in the years ahead. I know that in your previous role at DOT, you became very familiar with many of the issues regarding capital project delivery in New York City and worked closely with DDC on DOT's street reconstruction projects. Through your work with DDC

on street reconstruction projects, do you identify any issues or challenges with the capital delivery process that you're planning to address in your new role at DDC?

First of all, thank you, Chair, and I'm very excited to take on this role and I appreciate the kind words. Listen, I think the hardest part about street reconstruction is we don't know what we don't know. I think we want— we try to anticipate, or we tried to work with utilities to guess what is under our roads, but we sometimes encounter things that we never thought were there. And this is— it's not just a utility issue, it could also be a DEP issue. We— and sometimes that is what leads to sort of like changes and delays. But you're right. Listen, more coordination is always important. I would also say DOT and DEP have done a lot of work on their end. So in preparing really strong capital initiation packages so that by the time DDC gets them in and we go through the front-end planning process, there's very little back and forth. And I think we've– we at DOT, we beefed up and we increased the staffing of the planning process and the planning staff so that by the time the CPI gets to DDC, there

is sort of minimal back and forth. DEP has the same– and I really, really appreciate that work now at DDC because it's much easier to combine scopes from two CPIs and two packages that are well scoped, that are well estimated, and that have a lot of the requirements already in place for us to put them out for design and delivery.
What role do you think alternative project delivery methods could or should play for DOT street reconstruction projects?
You know, and I'm going to let our Associate Commissioner add anything if I miss it. By the way, it's his birthday.

Oh well, happy birthday. Commissioner Fletcher should have showed up on your behalf, sir. No, no, we thank you for coming. Happy birthday. Let's do a happy birthday chant, everybody. Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday, dear Igor, happy birthday to you. See, now I can't go that hard.

Okay, the best present you could get is being invited to this hearing. So I think we haven't done enough design-build projects of horizontal– of horizontal

nature. We have a handful of DB projects of DOT scope. I think the challenges are very similar. It is something that I'm going to be working on as new DDC Commissioner. I think we had done a really, really good job at vertical projects. I think we still have a bit more work to be done with DOT and with DEP to do more design-build for horizontal projects. It's something that I've spoken with our Deputy Commissioner Tom Wynne. He's very excited about it. It is still in its infancy compared to vertical projects, but I— that is one of my top priorities. And if it works, we're going to be expanding it for as many street reconstruction projects as we can. I would say though, we are doing design-build, I failed to mention, for ped ramps, which is working well, and raised crosswalks, but not in the typical street reconstruction way that I think you're asking.
And I think you said in your testimony that the design-build has already cut the— some projects by nearly half.
Yeah.

And I know still very early in our tracking of that, but it's something

that, you know, we're going to be want— we're going to want to monitor in years to come.
Yeah, that's right, that's right. And we appreciate your support. Every time there is a negotiation in Albany, the Council has always been supportive in home rules or anything else we may need.

Certainly, ensuring that the city's capital projects are delivered on time and within budget is complicated, particularly when it comes to large-scale projects. While DDC has taken a number of steps in recent years to improve project oversight and construction management practices, time and cost overruns continue to be two of the defining challenges of the city's capital program. In a December 2025 report, the Comptroller's Office reviewed a sample of 18 large-scale city projects and found that the construction costs were over budget by $370 million. If the results for the sampled projects were extrapolated across all large-scale projects, the total cost to the city for these projects would be an increase of approximately $870 million, or a 91 percent— or 9.1 percent. By your calculation, how frequently do projects exceed

their original amounts, their original budgets, and by how much on average?

Yeah, first of all, we appreciate Comptroller looking into this, and, you know, Comptroller Lander was a member of the Capital Delivery Task Force. There is a lot of recommendations in the Comptroller's report that we agree with. The timelines we disagree. The way that the timelines were measured, we don't agree. The timelines essentially were measured by the— before they started getting to DDC. Some of the budget overruns are scope changes, and so there's— and I'll be happy to brief you on that. There's a disagreements about how the data of that report was put out, but there's a lot of other recommendations that we agree with and we're already implementing for the comptrollers.

What are those disagreements? So essentially it's like, when does the project start is a disagreement. We believe that the project starts when it gets to DDC. The way that the Comptroller's Office— my understanding, they were counting the timing. The timing is when the projects were funded, which is a very different— a project

could be funded for a number of years outside the five-year window, for example. The sponsor agency could take sometimes years to put out a CPI before DDC gets it. And so the— when the clock starts is a key question.
Are you referring to rebasing?
I'm not familiar with rebasing.
Which I'll get into– I'll get into that later.
Okay.
Can you please provide a year-to-year comparison of the average project budget overrun?

I don't have that– I don't think I can provide that with you— for you today, but I am happy to look into it. I do want to push back on the overrun to make sure that we're talking about the same thing, because if it's scope changes, I would not cat— categorize those as cost overruns. That is a decision that the sponsor agency who's paying for the project is making to make sure

that the project delivered actually meets their standards.
Are agencies consistently conducting early enough due diligence to avoid preventable cost escalation?

No, no, not at all. No, no. Listen, it's a conversation that we have with sponsor agencies. I, you know, I think I mentioned DEP and DOT as sort of street reconstruction agencies. I know for a fact they've done a lot, a lot of work on the front end to avoid these difficult conversations or minimize the unknowns. On the front end. So I know on the street reconstruction side they're doing that. I know DCLA does that as well for cultural projects. I completely agree that I think we need to do a better job to touch the cultural institutions directly. But I think a lot of the agencies we work with are doing a lot of that front-end planning themselves to make sure that we limit delays once they get to us.
What are some reforms that would most effectively reduce cost increases without compromising project quality or safety?

Yeah, you know, a lot of the reforms put out in the Capital Reform Task Force were very helpful. DDC piloted an expanded work allowance to essentially minimize the approvals for change orders. That— so it's essentially registering a baked-in contingency into projects so that whenever we do run into issues or whenever there's an unforeseen field condition, we don't have to go back to the Comptroller's Office to register a change order and we can pay up front to the vendor. That has been really, really helpful. It's something, again, that DDC piloted. DOT is now implementing, and I believe other agencies as well. There's– there was a lot of procurement items in the Capital Reform Taskforce that were really helpful, things like electronic bidding. The city did not have that before. The public notice, the timelines for the public notice were also cut down. There's a lot of things that we– on the admin– that can be done on the admin side to reduce the actual timelines for project delivery.

I was going to ask questions later on the Capital Process Reform Taskforce, but since we're on it, I can skip to that

really briefly. Of the 39 Capital Process Reform Taskforce recommendations, how many have been fully implemented, how many are in progress, and how many remain outstanding?
My understanding is that fully implemented, about 24 with the rest— with the other 15 in progress.
So 24 have been implemented?
Yes, that is my understanding.
And you have the breakdown of– you know, I mean, there's a lot of them, but if you can send us that.

Yes, I do have– yes. We should have the breakdown, and I believe there's a progress report. Jeff can add, but there's a progress report every year on the individual recommendations and how the progress is being made. Oh, I have it.
Okay.
I can share it with you either now or at the end of the hearing.
Great. And Which ones have been the hardest to implement and which ones have produced the most measurable results so far?

Yeah, I think the hardest to implement usually are ones that the city themselves don't control, either require state legislation, or other forms of authority. But there's also some data, some recommendations that required new data systems that take a little while to build out. But I believe they're all underway. I have it in front of me. I'm happy to list them, but I can also just provide them.
I'll just— if you could just give that to us so that we can take back.

Sure. Oh, just one– I do want to call out one really, really important one, and I really liked this recommendation when I was at DOT, and I will eventually reap the benefits at DDC. It is the expansion of the CPSD process. It's the Capital Project Scope Development Fund that OMB manages. Essentially, it is money that OMB sets aside for really well-done capital scope projects, and this is— we essentially– the way it works is we present projects to OMB of things, ideas that we may have

that require more detailed scoping than what we traditionally would do in-house, and then those yield really good capital projects moving forward. At DOT, we did one for Flatlands Yard, one of our key yards, for the roadway divisions and the fleet division. And that will now— that is now going to be moving forward for a full capital project.
Thank you, Commissioner. Let me just move on to the other set of questions.
Sure.
I know you can go on for an extensive time on that.
Yes.
How– on average, how long are projects delayed beyond their initial projected completion dates?

Well, this is the one— this is the– it depends on— this is where we disagree with the Comptroller and how we categorize delays. I don't have an average with me. And again, there's sometimes factors outside of DDC's control that do cause delays. Sometimes there's legal issues or environmental issues. But I don't have an exact

timeline. Also, it depends on the type of project, if it's public buildings or infrastructure.

So the report also found that DDC— in a quote— DDC does not have a system capable of tracking real-time project costs from initiation to completion or for forecasting future costs across its project portfolio. DDC cannot readily determine the actual percentage of projects experiencing cost overruns and is unable to effectively monitor or report variances from original cost to completion cost on individual projects or an aggregate level. This deficiency resulted in a suspension of reporting project costs against original budget in the MMR from 2021 to 2024, end quote. How do you respond to this audit finding that DDC is unable to determine the actual percentage of projects experiencing cost overruns?

I'm going to partly disagree. So let me explain. The— it doesn't— we don't have a single system that does that. We have– Benchmark does sort of the project delivery, and we have systems for budget and cost. We track both. So I want to be very, very clear that we do track both. They're just not on the same system. And so what– the

commitment to DDC and to the Council and Comptroller is that I'm going to be looking at all systems and IT systems that the agency uses to make sure that we are giving our project managers all the tools they need for them to properly manage both the timelines and the cost. But I want to be very clear, we have systems for both. It is just not one single integrated system.
So is it fair to say that you are monitoring the actual cost of projects?
Yes, of course.
And so is it— is that just not being reported? Is that the conclusion?

That was one of the disagreements. My understanding was in going back and forth with the Comptroller's Office. And it's— I believe it's in our official response that was published as part of the report.
Do you commit to add these to future MMR reports?
The— if we can— if we can agree on what a benchmark looks like, then yes, I'm happy to have that conversation.
Well, what would be the— what are some benchmarks? Because this is just basic– we know– I think members of the public—
[interposing] Yeah, right.
want to know what these costs for projects are.

But the problem is like, it's building a new library versus building a, you know, a street project and a— or a water main project versus a full reconstruction project. They're just very different. And so we would— I would want to have, you know, benchmarks for every type of project, which can be a little complicated, but I'm sure we can come up with something.
Okay, so you're committed to come up with some kind of benchmarks?
